newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine parliament gives 1997 budget first reading.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine parliament gives 1997 budget first reading.

text.p: Ukraine's parliament on Thursday gave the first reading to a 1997 draft budget and gave the government two weeks to make changes to the document before presenting it to parliament again.

The draft, put forward by the budget committee, was a composite document distilled from two previous drafts -- one presented by the government in September and a tough November proposal issued by Deputy Minister of the Economy Viktor Pynzenyk with International Monetary Fund (IMF) approval.
"The budget commission has reached the conclusion that fundamental changes must be made to the budget project," the committee said in a resolution.
But deputies were not asked to vote on basic budget parameters such as spending and revenue plans.

Deputies voted 250 to 18 in favour of resolutions calling for larger revenues, a lower deficit, continuing benefits to victims of the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and war veterans, and greater allocations to industrial and agriculture sectors.
"This vote gives the government two weeks to work on the document and return it to us," Speaker Olexander Moroz told deputies after a 45-minute debate and vote.
The committee also requested changes to the two draft budgets already in circulation.
Even deputies expressed confusion over what was being voted on and Western diplomats have said it could take months to overcome the chaos.
Ukraine was initially slow to adopt market oriented reforms and parliament is dominated by conservatives who favour subsidies and Soviet-style handouts.

The country of 51 million people hopes for a $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility from the IMF, and some $5 billion in foreign grants and credits for the next three years depend on continued economic reforms.

Western funding bodies and economists have lauded the November draft, which predicted the republic's first post-Soviet economic growth of 1.7 percent compared to a forecast drop of 7.0 percent this year.

Budget Committee Chief Mykola Azarov has said previously that the committee wants a deficit of five percent, smaller than in the November budget which called for a deficit of 5.5 percent of GDP -- four percent by Western calculations.
The 1996 deficit is forecast at 6.2 percent.
He also said the inflation forecast of 25 percent for 1997 would remain, compared with a forecast 38 percent this year.
Thursday's vote means Ukraine will start the new year with the 1996 budget, although the constitution states that a new budget must be passed by January 1.
